Genetics points to a different river. A 2012 study in Nature sequenced 446 wild Oryza rufipogon plants and 1,083 cultivated varieties and concluded that japonica rice was first domesticated from a specific wild population around the middle Pearl River in southern China. In that model, indica rice, the long-grain type common across South and Southeast Asia, developed later as early japonica rice spread and crossed with local wild rice. The archaeology, meanwhile, keeps finding the oldest domestication evidence in the lower Yangtze, more than 1,000 km to the northeast. passages.text: History of rice cultivation The history of rice cultivation is an interdisciplinary subject that studies archaeological and documentary evidence to explain how rice was first domesticated and cultivated by humans, the spread of cultivation to different regions of the planet, and the technological changes that have impacted cultivation over time. The current scientific consensus, based on archaeological and linguistic evidence, is that Oryza sativa rice was first domesticated in the Yangtze River basin in China 9,000 years ago.[1][2][3][4] Cultivation, migration and trade spread rice around the world—first to much of East Asia, and then further abroad, and eventually to the Americas as part of the Columbian exchange. The now less common Oryza glaberrima rice, also known as African Rice, was independently domesticated in Africa around 3,000 years ago.[5] O. glaberrima spread to the Americas through the transatlantic slave trade although how is not clear. It is still commonly grown in West Africa and is grown in a number of countries in the Americas.[6][7] There are also several crosses of O. glaberrima and O. sativa.[8][9][10] Four species of rice that form the genus Zizania, commonly known as wild rice are native to and cultivated in North America, where the grain is

Wild rice and domesticated rice (Oryza sativa and Oryza glaberrima) belong to the same botanical tribe, Oryzeae.[11][12] Wild rice is also cultivated in Hungary and Australia.[13] Since its spread, rice has become a global staple crop important to food security and food cultures around the world. Local varieties of Oryza sativa have resulted in over 40,000 cultivars of various types. It was known to Greece (where it is still cultivated in Macedonia and Thrace) by returning soldiers from Alexander the Great's military expedition to Asia. Large deposits of rice from the first century AD have been found in Roman camps in Germany.[44] However, it was not a staple of the Greek diet until the 10th century. Prior to this, barley and wheat were the primary grains cultivated and consumed in Greece. Over time, rice gradually replaced these traditional grains as a staple ingredient in many Greek dishes. The Ummayad Caliphate brought Asiatic rice to the Iberian Peninsula in the 8th century where it expanded progressively from the south. Later studies suggested that the mutation arose in an ancestor of japonica rice first then found its way to indica. Since then, other teams have identified domestication genes that follow the same pattern: they appeared first in japonica before showing up in indica. One example is a mutation in a gene called Rc that lightened the seed coating, or pericarp3. These discoveries sent rice scientists scrambling to explain how indica and japonica could be genetically distinct across most of their genomes yet share mutations responsible for the key traits that made rice easier to cultivate. Although the specifics are still hotly contested, most researchers have concluded that human-directed hybridization played an important part in the very early history of domesticated rice. One leading theory comes from a 2011 study4 by Puruggunan and his colleagues that modelled the relationship of dozens of wild and domestic rice varieties. The study suggested that the domestication of japonica, most probably in China, was the watershed event in the history of Asian rice. passages.text: From a wild Asian grass to a refined crop that is the staple diet of half the world's population, the domestication of Oryza sativa spans centuries, but the grain's ancestry is hotly contested. Asian civilization was built on rice — on Oryza sativa, to be exact. The crop, which today is the primary food source for half of the world's population, transformed nomadic hunter-gatherers into stay-at-home farmers, spawned the first urban centres and built empires and dynasties. “Probably more so than any crop, it drove societies and economies to become densely populated, potentially more urbanized, and it also transformed landscapes,” says Dorian Fuller, an archaeobotanist at University College London. Despite — or possibly because of — rice's primacy, the history of the grain remains controversial, with little agreement on where, when and how many times humans tamed O. sativa in Asia to create the world's most important crop. (The only other domesticated rice species, Oryza glaberrima, has its roots in Africa. See 'The second story'.) “Almost every part of Asia had been pinpointed as the area where rice originated,” says Michael Purugganan, an evolutionary geneticist at New York University who studies rice domestication. passages.text: Where did rice come from? Asian rice, the rice most of the world eats, was domesticated in southern China from a wild grass, and the process took thousands of years. A study published in November 2026 from a site near Taihu Lake in the lower Yangtze adds fresh numbers to that story, showing domesticated rice slowly taking over a single village’s fields across three successive cultures. Here is what the archaeology and the genetics say, including the places where they still disagree. Quick answer: Asian rice came from a wild rice, Oryza rufipogon, in southern China. Rice remains from Shangshan in the lower Yangtze are about 9,400 years old and already look partly domesticated, but fully domesticated rice took thousands of years to win out. African rice is a separate crop, domesticated from a different wild rice in West Africa. Where did rice come from? Rice came from southern China. Asian rice, Oryza sativa, was domesticated from a wild rice called Oryza rufipogon, and the earliest evidence of people growing it comes from the lower Yangtze River valley in Zhejiang province. Where did African rice come from? African rice was domesticated in West Africa from the wild rice Oryza barthii. The inner Niger delta was long suggested as its center of origin, but a 2019 genomic study of 282 plants found that the key domestication mutations trace back to wild populations in several parts of West and Central Africa, and proposed that African rice came from a diffuse, multiregional process rather than one center. Later work continues to debate that. How to cook rice today All true rice is naturally gluten-free, a point our guide to whether rice is gluten-free covers in detail. Every later site shows wild and domesticated rice growing side by side for thousands of years, with the domesticated type slowly gaining ground. How do archaeologists tell wild rice from domesticated rice? They look at the spikelet base, the small scar where each grain attached to the plant. Wild rice shatters: ripe grains break off cleanly and fall to the ground to reseed, leaving a smooth scar. Domesticated rice does not shatter, so the grain has to be threshed off, which leaves a rough, torn base. Counting the two kinds in a pile of charred rice gives the share of domesticated plants in a harvest. The same shattering trait separates wild from domesticated wheat, as our post on where wheat came from explains. How long did rice domestication take? Thousands of years. From there it seems that japonica spread to India, where farmers intentionally hybridized it with their local rice to produce indica. The exact nature of that local rice is still a mystery. It could have been an early domesticated variety, or it could have been wild. Whether the creation of indica from japonica counts as a separate domestication event “is somewhat a semantic issue”, says Jeffrey Ross-Ibarra, an evolutionary geneticist at the University of California, Davis. The take-home message remains: the earliest fields of japonica — again, most probably in China — provided the key materials for the rice revolution in Asia. Origin stories Exactly where in China japonica was domesticated is another lively debate. The lower stretches of the Yangtze River valley in eastern China had long laid claim to early domestication, based on the discovery of roughly 8,000-year-old grains in archaeological sites there. passages.text: Rice dating methods place cultivation activities as far back as 9,000 years ago through the discovery of ancient rice grains, tools, and remains of domesticated rice cultivars. Independent Rice Domestication in Africa Around 3,000 years ago, a second rice plant species, Oryza glaberrima, or African rice, was independently domesticated along the Niger River in West Africa. The region surrounding the Niger River is considered the site of presumed domestication for Oryza glaberrima, where ancient communities independently developed rice cultivation techniques suited to local conditions. Unlike Asian domesticated rice (Oryza sativa), which spread widely, African rice remained regionally important, cultivated for its hardiness and local adaptability. Wild Grains in the Americas In North America, wild rices, particularly Zizania species, were harvested and cultivated by Native American communities, valued both as food and cultural heritage. Although genetically distinct from Oryza sativa, wild rice cultivation was vital for indigenous diets and cultural practices. The Evolution of Cultivated Rice Throughout the history of rice, farmers have selected for desirable early rice domestication traits such as non-shattering seed heads, larger rice grains, and higher rice yields to improve both harvest efficiency and food supply. Asian rice was domesticated from the wild rice Oryza rufipogon, according to a 2012 genome study of 446 wild and 1,083 cultivated plants. African rice comes from a different wild species, Oryza barthii. Is japonica or indica rice older? Japonica. The 2012 genome study found japonica was domesticated first in southern China, and indica developed later when japonica crossed with local wild rice in South and Southeast Asia. Is wild rice related to rice? Only distantly. North American wild rice belongs to a different genus of grasses, so it is not a wild form of the rice grown in Asia. How old is the oldest rice? The oldest dated rice remains, from Shangshan in China’s lower Yangtze, are about 9,400 years old.
